// Negative indexing (from end)
WITH [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] as nums
RETURN nums[-1] as last  // 5

docs.title: List Slicing
docs.text:
WITH [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] as nums
RETURN nums[1..3]  // [2, 3] (exclusive end)
RETURN nums[2..]   // [3, 4, 5] (to end)
RETURN nums[..3]   // [1, 2, 3] (from start)

docs.title: size()
docs.text:
Returns the number of elements in a list.

// Size of list
RETURN size([1, 2, 3])  // 3
RETURN size([])         // 0

// Size of string (number of characters)
RETURN size('Hello')    // 5

docs.title: head(), tail(), last()
docs.text:
WITH [1, 2, 3, 4] as list
RETURN head(list)  // 1  (first element)
RETURN last(list)  // 4  (last element)
RETURN tail(list)  // [2, 3, 4]  (all except first)

// With empty list
RETURN head([])    // null
RETURN last([])    // null
RETURN tail([])    // []

docs.title: reverse()
docs.text:
RETURN reverse([1, 2, 3])     // [3, 2, 1]
RETURN reverse(['a', 'b'])    // ['b', 'a']
RETURN reverse([])            // []

docs.title: range()
docs.text:
Generates a list of integers within a range.

// Basic range (inclusive)
RETURN range(1, 5)            // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
RETURN range(0, 3)            // [0, 1, 2, 3]

// With step
RETURN range(0, 10, 2)        // [0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
RETURN range(0, 9, 3)         // [0, 3, 6, 9]

// Negative step (descending)
RETURN range(5, 0, -1)        // [5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0]
RETURN range(10, 0, -2)       // [10, 8, 6, 4, 2, 0]

// Single element
RETURN range(5, 5)            // [5]

// Step cannot be zero
// RETURN range(1, 5, 0)      // ERROR

docs.title: List Comprehensions
docs.text:
// Filter and transform
WITH [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] as nums
RETURN [x IN nums WHERE x > 2 | x * 10] as result
// [30, 40, 50]

// Extract only
RETURN [x IN [1, 2, 3] | x * 2]  // [2, 4, 6]

// Filter only
RETURN [x IN [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] WHERE x > 2]  // [3, 4, 5]

docs.title: List Predicates
docs.text:
// ALL
WITH [1, 2, 3] as nums
RETURN ALL(x IN nums WHERE x > 0)  // true

// ANY
WITH [1, -1, 2] as nums
RETURN ANY(x IN nums WHERE x < 0)  // true

// NONE
WITH [1, 2, 3] as nums
RETURN NONE(x IN nums WHERE x < 0)  // true

// SINGLE
WITH [1, 2, 1] as nums
RETURN SINGLE(x IN nums WHERE x = 2)  // true

docs.title: Reducing Lists
docs.text:
// Sum all elements
WITH [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] as nums
RETURN reduce(sum = 0, x IN nums | sum + x)  // 15

// Build string
WITH ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'] as names
RETURN reduce(s = '', name IN names | s + ', ' + name)  // ', Alice, Bob, Charlie'

docs.title: Property Access on Lists of Nodes
docs.text:
When you have a list of nodes or relationships, you can access a property directly on the list to get a list of property values:

// Get names of all friends in one expression
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
WITH [(p)-[:KNOWS]->(f) | f] as friends
RETURN friends.name    // ['Bob', 'Charlie', 'David']

// Works with any property
MATCH (p:Person)
WITH collect(p) as persons
RETURN persons.age     // [25, 30, 35, ...]

This is equivalent to using a list comprehension:

// These are equivalent:
WITH friends, friends.name as names1
WITH friends, [f IN friends | f.name] as names2
// names1 == names2

Null handling

If any node in the list doesn't have the property, null is included in the result list.

docs.title: Creating Maps
docs.text:
// Literal map
RETURN {name: 'Alice', age: 30} as person

// Nested maps
RETURN {
  name: 'Alice',
  address: {city: 'NYC', zip: '10001'}
} as data

docs.title: Map Access
docs.text:
WITH {name: 'Alice', age: 30} as person
RETURN person.name, person.age
// Can also use: person['name']

docs.title: keys()
docs.text:
Returns a list of all keys in a map, or all property names of a node/relationship.

// Map keys
WITH {a: 1, b: 2, c: 3} as m
RETURN keys(m)    // ['a', 'b', 'c']

// Node property keys
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
RETURN keys(p)    // ['name', 'age', 'email', ...]

// Relationship property keys
MATCH ()-[r:KNOWS]->()
RETURN keys(r)    // ['since', ...]

docs.title: values()
docs.text:
Returns a list of all values in a map, or all property values of a node/relationship.

// Map values
WITH {a: 1, b: 2, c: 3} as m
RETURN values(m)  // [1, 2, 3]

// Node property values
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
RETURN values(p)  // ['Alice', 30, 'alice@example.com', ...]

docs.title: Dynamic Key Access
docs.text:
// Using variable as key
WITH {name: 'Alice'} as p, 'name' as key
RETURN p[key]  // 'Alice'

// Iterate over all properties
MATCH (p:Person)
WITH p, keys(p) as props
UNWIND props as key
RETURN p.name, key, p[key] as value

docs.title: Dynamic Property Access
docs.text:
// Get all property values
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN p.name, [key IN keys(p) | p[key]] as allValues

docs.title: Converting to Map
docs.text:
// Node to map
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
RETURN apoc.map.fromPairs([
  key IN keys(p) | [key, p[key]]
]) as personMap

docs.title: UNWIND
docs.text:
Expands lists into rows.

// Create nodes from list
UNWIND ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'] as name
CREATE (p:Person {name: name})

// Process list property
MATCH (p:Person)
UNWIND p.tags as tag
RETURN p.name, tag

// With multiple properties
MATCH (p:Person)
UNWIND p.interests as interest
WITH p, interest
WHERE interest.category = 'tech'
RETURN p.name, interest.name

docs.title: CREATE and MATCH
docs.text: The two most fundamental Cypher operations: creating data and finding data.

docs.title: CREATE
docs.text: Creates nodes and relationships.

docs.title: Create Nodes
docs.text:
// Simple node
CREATE (n)

// With label
CREATE (p:Person)

// With multiple labels
CREATE (p:Person:Employee)

// With properties
CREATE (p:Person {name: 'Alice', age: 30})

// With complex properties
CREATE (p:Person {
    name: 'Bob',
    tags: ['developer', 'python'],
    metadata: {joined: '2024-01-15'}
})

docs.title: Create Relationships
docs.text:
// Create both nodes and relationship
CREATE (a:Person {name: 'Alice'})-[:KNOWS]->(b:Person {name: 'Bob'})

// Create relationship between existing nodes
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Alice'}), (b:Person {name: 'Bob'})
CREATE (a)-[:KNOWS {since: 2020}]->(b)

// Create multiple relationships
CREATE (a)-[:KNOWS]->(b)-[:KNOWS]->(c)

docs.title: Create Multiple Elements
docs.text:
// Separate with commas
CREATE
  (a:Person {name: 'Alice'}),
  (b:Person {name: 'Bob'}),
  (c:Company {name: 'TechCorp'}),
  (a)-[:KNOWS]->(b),
  (a)-[:WORKS_AT]->(c)

docs.title: Create and Return
docs.text:
CREATE (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
RETURN p

docs.title: MATCH
docs.text: Finds existing patterns in the graph.

docs.title: Match Nodes
docs.text:
// Any node
MATCH (n)
RETURN n

// By label
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN p

// By multiple labels
MATCH (p:Person:Employee)
RETURN p

// By property
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
RETURN p

// By multiple properties
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice', age: 30})
RETURN p

docs.title: Match Relationships
docs.text:
// Any relationship
MATCH ()-[r]->()
RETURN r

// By type
MATCH ()-[r:KNOWS]->()
RETURN r

// With direction
MATCH (a)-[r:KNOWS]->(b)
RETURN a.name, b.name

// Both directions
MATCH (a)-[r:KNOWS]-(b)
RETURN a.name, b.name

// Specific nodes
MATCH (a:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->(b:Person)
RETURN a.name, b.name

docs.title: Match with Properties
docs.text:
// Properties in pattern
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})-[:KNOWS]->(friend)
RETURN friend.name

// Properties on relationship
MATCH (a)-[r:WORKS_AT {since: 2020}]->(b)
RETURN a.name, b.name

docs.title: Connect Existing Nodes
docs.text:
# First create nodes
db.execute("""
    CREATE (a:Person {name: 'Alice'}),
           (b:Person {name: 'Bob'})
""")

# Then connect them
db.execute("""
    MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Alice'}), (b:Person {name: 'Bob'})
    CREATE (a)-[:KNOWS {since: 2020}]->(b)
""")

docs.title: Find or Create Pattern
docs.text:
Use MERGE for find-or-create (see Data Modification):

MERGE (p:Person {email: 'alice@example.com'})
ON CREATE SET p.name = 'Alice', p.created = datetime()
ON MATCH SET p.lastSeen = datetime()
RETURN p

docs.title: Fixed Length
docs.text:
// Exactly 2 hops (friends of friends)
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Alice'})-[:KNOWS*2]->(fof)
RETURN fof

docs.title: Range
docs.text:
// 1 to 3 hops
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Alice'})-[:KNOWS*1..3]->(other)
RETURN other

docs.title: Unbounded
docs.text:
Uses default max hops configured at database creation:

db = GrafitoDatabase(':memory:', cypher_max_hops=5)

// Uses default max hops
MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS*..]->(other)
RETURN other

docs.title: Shortest Path
docs.text:
// Single shortest path
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Person {name: 'Alice'})-[:KNOWS*1..5]->(b:Person {name: 'Bob'})
)
RETURN p, length(p) as hops

// All shortest paths
MATCH p = allShortestPaths(
  (a:Person {name: 'Alice'})-[:KNOWS*1..5]->(b:Person {name: 'Bob'})
)
RETURN p

docs.title: Pattern Comprehensions
docs.text:
Collect related nodes in a list:

// Get Alice's friends as a list
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Alice'})
RETURN [(a)-[:KNOWS]->(b) | b.name] as friends

// With filter
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Alice'})
RETURN [(a)-[:KNOWS]->(b) WHERE b.active | b.name] as activeFriends

docs.title: Social Network
docs.text:
// Friends of friends
MATCH (me:Person {name: 'Alice'})-[:KNOWS]->()-[:KNOWS]->(fof)
WHERE fof <> me
RETURN DISTINCT fof.name

docs.title: Organization Hierarchy
docs.text:
// All reports to a manager
MATCH (mgr:Person {name: 'Alice'})<-[:REPORTS_TO*]-(emp)
RETURN emp.name

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
// People with similar interests
MATCH (me:Person)-[:INTERESTED_IN]->(interest)<-[:INTERESTED_IN]-(other)
WHERE me.name = 'Alice' AND other <> me
RETURN other.name, count(interest) as common
ORDER BY common DESC

docs.title: Filtering with WHERE
docs.text: The WHERE clause filters results from MATCH operations.

docs.title: Comparison Operators
docs.text:
// Equal
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.name = 'Alice'
RETURN p

// Not equal
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.name <> 'Alice'
RETURN p

// Greater than
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.age > 25
RETURN p.name

// Greater or equal
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.age >= 18
RETURN p.name

// Less than
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.age < 65
RETURN p.name

// Less or equal
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.age <= 30
RETURN p.name

docs.title: Range Comparisons
docs.text:
// Chained comparisons
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE 18 <= p.age <= 65
RETURN p.name

// Equivalent to:
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.age >= 18 AND p.age <= 65
RETURN p.name

docs.title: AND
docs.text:
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.age > 25 AND p.city = 'NYC'
RETURN p.name

docs.title: OR
docs.text:
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.city = 'NYC' OR p.city = 'LA'
RETURN p.name

docs.title: NOT
docs.text:
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE NOT p.active
RETURN p.name

// Can also use for negation
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE NOT (p.age > 25)
RETURN p.name

docs.title: Combining Operators
docs.text:
// Use parentheses for clarity
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE (p.age > 25 AND p.city = 'NYC') OR p.city = 'LA'
RETURN p.name

// Complex condition
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.active = true
  AND (p.age < 25 OR p.age > 65)
  AND NOT p.name = 'Admin'
RETURN p.name

docs.title: IS NULL / IS NOT NULL
docs.text:
// Find persons without age
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.age IS NULL
RETURN p.name

// Find persons with age set
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.age IS NOT NULL
RETURN p.name, p.age

docs.title: NULL Comparisons
docs.text:
// NULL comparisons return NULL (falsy in WHERE)
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.age = NULL  // This never matches!
RETURN p

// Correct way
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.age IS NULL
RETURN p

docs.title: Three-Valued Logic (True/False/Null)
docs.text: Cypher uses three-valued logic for boolean operations involving null:

docs.title: AND Operator
docs.text:
Left Right Result true true true true false false true null null false any false null false false null true null null null null 
// Examples
RETURN true AND true      // true
RETURN true AND null      // null
RETURN false AND null     // false
RETURN null AND null      // null

docs.title: OR Operator
docs.text:
Left Right Result true any true false false false false true true false null null null true true null false null null null null 
// Examples
RETURN true OR null       // true
RETURN false OR null      // null
RETURN null OR false      // null
RETURN null OR true       // true

docs.title: IN Operator with NULL
docs.text:
// Value exists in list
RETURN 2 IN [1, 2, 3]           // true

// Value doesn't exist
RETURN 5 IN [1, 2, 3]           // false

// List contains NULL
RETURN 5 IN [1, 2, null]        // null (might exist, unknown)
RETURN 2 IN [1, 2, null]        // true (definitely exists)

// NULL value
RETURN null IN [1, 2, 3]        // null

docs.title: STARTS WITH
docs.text:
// Names starting with 'Al'
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.name STARTS WITH 'Al'
RETURN p.name

docs.title: ENDS WITH
docs.text:
// Emails ending with '@company.com'
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.email ENDS WITH '@company.com'
RETURN p.name

docs.title: CONTAINS
docs.text:
// Names containing 'li'
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.name CONTAINS 'li'
RETURN p.name

docs.title: Regular Expressions
docs.text:
// Regexp matching
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.name =~ '^A.*e$'
RETURN p.name

// Case insensitive (with (?i))
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.name =~ '(?i)^alice$'
RETURN p.name

docs.title: List-Scalar Comparisons
docs.text:
When comparing a list with a scalar value using = or !=, Cypher checks if the value exists in the list:

// Check if scalar equals any element in list
WITH [1, 2, 3] as nums
WHERE nums = 2
RETURN 'found'      // 'found' - 2 is in the list

// Check if scalar is not in list
WITH [1, 2, 3] as nums
WHERE nums != 5
RETURN 'not found'  // 'not found' - 5 is not in the list

// Works with nodes too
MATCH (p:Person)
WITH collect(p) as persons
WHERE persons = 'Alice'    // true if any person is named Alice
RETURN persons

Only = and !=

This shorthand only works with equality (=) and inequality (!=) operators, not with <, >, etc.

docs.title: IN Operator
docs.text:
// Match any of these names
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.name IN ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie']
RETURN p.name

// Check if value in list property
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE 'developer' IN p.tags
RETURN p.name

docs.title: List Predicates
docs.text:
// All elements satisfy condition
WITH [1, 2, 3] as list
WHERE ALL(x IN list WHERE x > 0)
RETURN list

// Any element satisfies condition
WITH [1, -1, 2] as list
WHERE ANY(x IN list WHERE x < 0)
RETURN list

// No element satisfies condition
WITH [1, 2, 3] as list
WHERE NONE(x IN list WHERE x < 0)
RETURN list

// Exactly one element satisfies condition
WITH [1, 2, 3] as list
WHERE SINGLE(x IN list WHERE x = 2)
RETURN list

docs.title: Label Predicates
docs.text:
Test a node's labels directly in WHERE with n:Label. Chain labels with : to require all of them, and combine with NOT, AND, OR like any boolean:

// Nodes carrying the Admin label
MATCH (n)
WHERE n:Admin
RETURN n.name

// Both labels required
MATCH (n)
WHERE n:Person:Admin
RETURN n.name

// Negation and combination
MATCH (n)
WHERE NOT n:Reference AND (n:ADR OR n:Term)
RETURN n.title

The same predicate can be projected as a boolean in RETURN:

MATCH (n:Person {name: 'Alice'})
RETURN n:Admin AS is_admin

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Use $name parameters instead of interpolating values into the WHERE condition (see Query Parameters):

MATCH (n:Person)
WHERE n.age >= $min_age AND n.name IN $names
RETURN n.name

db.execute(query, {"min_age": 18, "names": ["Alice", "Bob"]})

docs.title: Pattern Filtering
docs.text:
A pattern can be used directly as a truth value: it is true when it matches at least once, holding fixed whatever variables are already bound.

// Persons who know someone
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE (p)-[:KNOWS]->()
RETURN p.name

// ...and the reason this exists: persons who know nobody
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE NOT (p)-[:KNOWS]->()
RETURN p.name

Matching stops at the first hit, so a node with thousands of neighbours costs the same as one with a single edge — unlike counting them.

docs.title: What the Pattern Can Contain
docs.text:
Anything MATCH accepts: types, labels, direction, inline properties, and variable-length paths.

WHERE (p)-[:WORKS_AT]->(:Company)          // label on the far node
WHERE (p)-[:KNOWS {since: 2020}]->()       // property on the relationship
WHERE (p)-->({age: 30})                    // property on the far node
WHERE ()-[:REPORTS_TO]->(p)                // incoming
WHERE (p)--()                              // either direction
WHERE (p)-[*1..3]->(:Company)              // within three hops
WHERE (p)-->()-->(:Company)                // multi-hop

Variables already bound by the surrounding query keep their values, so a pattern over two of them asks about those specific nodes:

MATCH (p:Person), (c:Company {name: 'Acme'})
WHERE NOT (p)-[:WORKS_AT]->(c)
RETURN p.name          // everyone who does not work at Acme

docs.title: EXISTS
docs.text:
EXISTS() over a pattern means the same thing, and reads better when combined with other predicates:

MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE EXISTS((p)-[:KNOWS]->()) AND p.age > 30
RETURN p.name

Note that EXISTS() is overloaded: given a property it tests for presence (see Property Existence), given a pattern it tests for a match.

docs.title: As a Value
docs.text:
A pattern predicate is an ordinary boolean expression, so it can be returned or projected:

MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN p.name, (p)-[:KNOWS]->() AS is_connected

To count matches rather than test for one, use a pattern comprehension:

MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN p.name, size([(p)-[:KNOWS]->(f) | f]) AS friends

Filtering on a WITH alias

WITH n, (n)-->() AS connected WHERE connected does not work — and not because of patterns: referring to a WITH alias inside that same clause's WHERE is unsupported for any expression. Filter in a following clause:

MATCH (n:Person)
WITH n
WHERE (n)-[:KNOWS]->()
RETURN n.name

docs.title: Property Existence
docs.text:
// Using EXISTS for property (alternate to IS NOT NULL)
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE EXISTS(p.email)
RETURN p.name

// Combined with value check
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE EXISTS(p.age) AND p.age > 25
RETURN p.name

docs.title: User Management
docs.text:
// Active users with verified email
MATCH (u:User)
WHERE u.active = true
  AND u.emailVerified = true
  AND u.createdAt > date('2024-01-01')
RETURN u.email

docs.title: Product Search
docs.text:
// Available products in category
MATCH (p:Product)
WHERE p.category IN ['electronics', 'computers']
  AND p.stock > 0
  AND (p.price >= 100 AND p.price <= 500)
RETURN p.name, p.price

docs.title: Social Network
docs.text:
// Active friends in same city
MATCH (me:Person {name: 'Alice'})-[:KNOWS]->(friend)
WHERE friend.active = true
  AND friend.city = me.city
  AND NOT friend.name = me.name
RETURN friend.name

docs.title: Indexes and Constraints
docs.text: Schema management for performance and data integrity.

docs.title: Creating Node Indexes
docs.text:
Programmatic API:

db.create_node_index('Person', 'name')
db.create_node_index('Person', 'email')  # Can index same label different props

Cypher:

// Modern syntax
CREATE INDEX FOR (n:Person) ON (n.name)

// Alternative syntax
CREATE INDEX FOR NODE :Person(name)

// With explicit name
CREATE INDEX person_email_idx FOR (n:Person) ON (n.email)

docs.title: Creating Relationship Indexes
docs.text:
Programmatic API:

db.create_relationship_index('KNOWS', 'since')

Cypher:

// Modern syntax
CREATE INDEX FOR ()-[r:KNOWS]-() ON (r.since)

// Alternative syntax
CREATE INDEX FOR RELATIONSHIP :KNOWS(since)

docs.title: IF NOT EXISTS
docs.text:
// Skip if already exists
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:Person) ON (n.name)

docs.title: Unique Indexes
docs.text: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX FOR (n:User) ON (n.email)

docs.title: URI Indexes
docs.text:
For URI/URL-based lookups:

# Programmatic
db.create_node_uri_index()
db.create_relationship_uri_index()

// Cypher
CALL db.uri_index.create('node')
CALL db.uri_index.create('relationship')

docs.title: Listing Indexes
docs.text:
# Programmatic
indexes = db.list_indexes()
for idx in indexes:
    print(f"{idx['name']}: {idx['entity']}:{idx['label_or_type']}({idx['property']})")

// All indexes
SHOW INDEXES

// Filtered
SHOW INDEXES WHERE entity = 'node'
SHOW INDEXES WHERE label_or_type = 'Person'

docs.title: Dropping Indexes
docs.text:
db.drop_index('idx_node_person_name')

// By name
DROP INDEX idx_node_person_name

// If exists
DROP INDEX IF EXISTS idx_node_person_name

docs.title: Uniqueness Constraints
docs.text:
// Node property must be unique (nulls allowed)
CREATE CONSTRAINT FOR (n:User) REQUIRE n.email IS UNIQUE

// With name
CREATE CONSTRAINT user_email_unique FOR (n:User) REQUIRE n.email IS UNIQUE

docs.title: Existence Constraints
docs.text:
// Property must exist on all nodes with label
CREATE CONSTRAINT FOR (n:Person) REQUIRE n.name IS NOT NULL

docs.title: Type Constraints
docs.text:
// Property must be of specific type
CREATE CONSTRAINT FOR (n:Person) REQUIRE n.age IS INTEGER
CREATE CONSTRAINT FOR (n:User) REQUIRE n.active IS BOOLEAN
CREATE CONSTRAINT FOR (n:Product) REQUIRE n.price IS FLOAT
CREATE CONSTRAINT FOR (n:Document) REQUIRE n.tags IS LIST
CREATE CONSTRAINT FOR (n:Config) REQUIRE n.settings IS MAP
CREATE CONSTRAINT FOR (n:User) REQUIRE n.bio IS STRING

Supported types: STRING, INTEGER, FLOAT, BOOLEAN, LIST, MAP

docs.title: Relationship Constraints
docs.text:
// All work relationships must have 'since' property
CREATE CONSTRAINT FOR ()-[r:WORKS_AT]-() REQUIRE r.since IS NOT NULL

// Type constraint on relationship property
CREATE CONSTRAINT FOR ()-[r:KNOWS]-() REQUIRE r.strength IS INTEGER

docs.title: Neo4j-Style Syntax
docs.text:
// Alternative syntax for compatibility
CREATE CONSTRAINT FOR (n:Person) ON (n.email) IS UNIQUE
CREATE CONSTRAINT FOR (n:Person) ON (n.age) IS INTEGER

docs.title: Listing Constraints
docs.text:
// All constraints
SHOW CONSTRAINTS

// Filtered
SHOW CONSTRAINTS WHERE entity = 'node'
SHOW CONSTRAINTS WHERE type = 'uniqueness'

docs.title: Dropping Constraints
docs.text:
// By auto-generated name
DROP CONSTRAINT constraint_node_person_email_unique

// By custom name
DROP CONSTRAINT user_email_unique

// If exists
DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS user_email_unique

docs.title: Uniqueness and NULL
docs.text:
// NULL values are not checked for uniqueness
CREATE CONSTRAINT FOR (n:User) REQUIRE n.email IS UNIQUE

// These are both valid:
CREATE (u1:User {name: 'Alice'})  // email is null
CREATE (u2:User {name: 'Bob'})    // email is null (also null, allowed!)

// But this would fail:
CREATE (u3:User {email: 'a@b.com'})
CREATE (u4:User {email: 'a@b.com'})  // ERROR: duplicate

docs.title: Type Constraints Require Non-NULL
docs.text:
CREATE CONSTRAINT FOR (n:Person) REQUIRE n.age IS INTEGER

// This fails - age is NULL
CREATE (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})

// This works
CREATE (p:Person {name: 'Alice', age: 30})

// This fails - wrong type
CREATE (p:Person {name: 'Bob', age: 'thirty'})

docs.title: When to Create Indexes
docs.text:
-- Index properties used in:
-- 1. MATCH lookups
CREATE INDEX FOR (n:User) ON (n.email)

-- 2. WHERE filters
CREATE INDEX FOR (n:Product) ON (n.category)

-- 3. ORDER BY
CREATE INDEX FOR (n:Post) ON (n.created_at)

docs.title: Index Strategy
docs.text:
# Don't index everything - each index has overhead
# Index properties that are:
# - Frequently queried
# - High cardinality (many unique values)
# - Used for sorting

# Good candidates:
db.create_node_index('User', 'email')      # Unique lookup
db.create_node_index('Order', 'order_id')  # ID lookup

# Poor candidates:
# db.create_node_index('User', 'active')   # Low cardinality (true/false)
# db.create_node_index('Log', 'message')   # Never queried directly

docs.title: Constraints First
docs.text:
-- Create constraints before importing data
-- Data with violations will be rejected

CREATE CONSTRAINT FOR (n:User) REQUIRE n.email IS UNIQUE;
CREATE CONSTRAINT FOR (n:User) REQUIRE n.name IS NOT NULL;

-- Now import data
CREATE (u:User {email: 'alice@example.com', name: 'Alice'});

docs.title: Constraint Violation
docs.text:
ConstraintError: Node(123) already exists with label `User` and `email` = 'alice@example.com'

Solution: Use MERGE instead of CREATE for upsert semantics.

docs.title: Index Not Used
docs.text:
-- Some queries can't use indexes
-- Pattern expressions in WHERE
WHERE (p)-[:KNOWS]->()  -- Can't use index on p

-- Functions on indexed property
WHERE toUpper(p.name) = 'ALICE'  -- Won't use index

-- Instead, normalize on insert:
SET p.name_lower = toLower(p.name)
-- Then query:
WHERE p.name_lower = 'alice'

docs.title: Data Modification
docs.text: Modifying existing data with SET, DELETE, REMOVE, and MERGE.

docs.title: SET
docs.text: Updates properties on nodes and relationships.

docs.title: Set Single Property
docs.text:
// Set one property
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
SET p.age = 31

docs.title: Set Multiple Properties
docs.text:
// Set multiple properties
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
SET p.city = 'NYC', p.country = 'USA'

docs.title: Set from Map
docs.text:
// Replace all properties using =
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
SET p = {name: 'Alice', age: 31, city: 'NYC'}

// This removes all other properties!

docs.title: Add/Update Properties with +=
docs.text:
// Merge properties (add new, update existing, keep others)
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
SET p += {city: 'NYC', department: 'Engineering'}

docs.title: Set with Expression
docs.text:
// Increment value
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
SET p.loginCount = p.loginCount + 1

// Set from calculation
MATCH (p:Person)
SET p.ageNextYear = p.age + 1

docs.title: Set with CREATE/MATCH
docs.text:
// Create and set in one
CREATE (p:Person)
SET p.name = 'Bob', p.age = 25

docs.title: DELETE
docs.text: Removes nodes and relationships.

docs.title: Delete Relationship
docs.text:
// Delete specific relationship
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Alice'})-[r:KNOWS]->(b:Person {name: 'Bob'})
DELETE r

docs.title: Delete Node
docs.text:
// Delete node (must detach relationships first)
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
DELETE p

docs.title: DETACH DELETE
docs.text:
// Delete node and all its relationships
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
DETACH DELETE p

docs.title: Delete Multiple
docs.text:
// Delete multiple items
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})-[r]-(), (p)
DELETE r, p

docs.title: REMOVE
docs.text: Removes labels and properties.

docs.title: Remove Property
docs.text:
// Remove single property
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
REMOVE p.temporary

// Remove multiple properties
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
REMOVE p.temp1, p.temp2

docs.title: Remove Label
docs.text:
// Remove single label
MATCH (p:Person:Employee {name: 'Alice'})
REMOVE p:Employee

// Remove multiple labels
MATCH (p:Person:Employee:Manager {name: 'Alice'})
REMOVE p:Employee, p:Manager
// Now p only has :Person label

docs.title: Remove All Labels
docs.text:
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
REMOVE p:Person
// Node now has no labels

docs.title: MERGE
docs.text: Finds existing patterns or creates them if not found.

docs.title: Basic MERGE
docs.text:
// Find or create node
MERGE (p:Person {email: 'alice@example.com'})
RETURN p

docs.title: MERGE with ON CREATE
docs.text:
// Set properties only when creating
MERGE (p:Person {email: 'alice@example.com'})
ON CREATE SET
  p.name = 'Alice',
  p.createdAt = datetime(),
  p.active = true
RETURN p

docs.title: MERGE with ON MATCH
docs.text:
// Update properties only when existing
MERGE (p:Person {email: 'alice@example.com'})
ON MATCH SET
  p.lastSeen = datetime(),
  p.visitCount = p.visitCount + 1
RETURN p

docs.title: Combined ON CREATE and ON MATCH
docs.text:
MERGE (p:Person {email: 'alice@example.com'})
ON CREATE SET
  p.name = 'Alice',
  p.createdAt = datetime()
ON MATCH SET
  p.lastSeen = datetime()
RETURN p

docs.title: MERGE Relationship
docs.text:
// Find or create relationship
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Alice'}), (b:Person {name: 'Bob'})
MERGE (a)-[r:KNOWS]->(b)
RETURN r

// With properties
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Alice'}), (b:Person {name: 'Bob'})
MERGE (a)-[r:KNOWS]->(b)
ON CREATE SET r.since = 2020
RETURN r

docs.title: MERGE Path
docs.text:
// Create entire path if not exists
MERGE (a:Person {name: 'Alice'})-[:KNOWS]->(b:Person {name: 'Bob'})
RETURN a, b

docs.title: MERGE with Multiple Patterns
docs.text:
// Match/create both nodes and relationship
MERGE (a:Person {email: 'alice@example.com'})
MERGE (b:Person {email: 'bob@example.com'})
MERGE (a)-[:KNOWS]->(b)

docs.title: FOREACH
docs.text:
Iterate over a list and perform operations.

// Set property on each element
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
FOREACH (tag IN ['developer', 'python', 'database'] |
  CREATE (t:Tag {name: tag})
  MERGE (p)-[:INTERESTED_IN]->(t)
)

docs.title: Upsert Pattern
docs.text:
// Update or insert (upsert)
MERGE (p:Person {email: $email})
ON CREATE SET
  p.name = $name,
  p.createdAt = datetime(),
  p.version = 1
ON MATCH SET
  p.name = $name,
  p.updatedAt = datetime(),
  p.version = p.version + 1
RETURN p

docs.title: Soft Delete
docs.text:
// Instead of DELETE, mark as inactive
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
SET p.active = false, p.deletedAt = datetime()
REMOVE p:Active

docs.title: Bulk Update
docs.text:
// Update many nodes at once
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.lastLogin < datetime() - duration('P1Y')
SET p.status = 'inactive'

docs.title: Property Migration
docs.text:
// Rename property
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE EXISTS(p.oldName)
SET p.newName = p.oldName
REMOVE p.oldName

docs.title: Numeric Functions
docs.text: Grafito's Cypher supports the standard mathematical functions and operators. All functions return null when given a null argument.

docs.title: Arithmetic Operators
docs.text:
Operator Meaning Example Result + Addition RETURN 2 + 3 AS r 5 - Subtraction RETURN 5 - 2 AS r 3 * Multiplication RETURN 4 * 3 AS r 12 / Division RETURN 10 / 3 AS r 3 % Modulo RETURN 10 % 3 AS r 1 ^ Exponentiation RETURN 2 ^ 10 AS r 1024.0

Division of two integers performs integer division (10 / 3 is 3); if either operand is a float the result is a float (10.0 / 4 is 2.5). Exponentiation always returns a float and is right-associative (2 ^ 2 ^ 3 is 2 ^ 8 = 256.0).

RETURN 2 + 3 * 4 AS r        // 14  (multiplication binds tighter)
RETURN (2 + 3) * 4 AS r      // 20

Dividing or taking the modulo by zero raises an error.

docs.title: abs()
docs.text:
Absolute value.

RETURN abs(-5) AS r   // 5

docs.title: ceil() / floor() / round()
docs.text:
ceil() rounds up, floor() rounds down, and round() rounds half away from zero (so round(2.5) is 3.0 and round(-2.5) is -3.0). All return floats.

RETURN ceil(1.2) AS r    // 2.0
RETURN floor(1.8) AS r   // 1.0
RETURN round(2.5) AS r   // 3.0

docs.title: sign()
docs.text:
Returns -1, 0, or 1 for negative, zero, or positive numbers.

RETURN sign(-3) AS r   // -1

docs.title: sqrt()
docs.text:
Square root. Raises an error for negative arguments.

RETURN sqrt(9) AS r   // 3.0

docs.title: exp() / log() / log10()
docs.text:
exp(x) is e raised to x; log(x) is the natural logarithm; log10(x) is the base-10 logarithm. log() and log10() require a positive argument.

RETURN exp(1) AS r     // 2.718281828459045
RETURN log10(1000) AS r  // 3.0

docs.title: Trigonometry
docs.text:
sin(), cos(), tan(), cot(), asin(), acos(), atan(), and atan2(y, x) operate in radians. asin() and acos() require an argument in [-1, 1]. degrees() and radians() convert between units, and haversin() returns (1 - cos(x)) / 2.

RETURN sin(0) AS r           // 0.0
RETURN asin(1) AS r          // 1.5707963267948966
RETURN atan2(1, 1) AS r      // 0.7853981633974483
RETURN degrees(pi()) AS r    // 180.0
RETURN radians(180) AS r     // 3.141592653589793

docs.title: e() / pi()
docs.text:
RETURN e() AS r    // 2.718281828459045
RETURN pi() AS r   // 3.141592653589793

docs.title: rand()
docs.text:
Returns a random float in [0, 1).

RETURN rand() AS r

docs.title: Numeric Casting
docs.text:
toInteger() and toFloat() convert numbers and numeric strings; see String Functions for details. For element-wise list casting, toIntegerList() / toFloatList() turn each convertible element and leave non-convertible ones as null.

RETURN toInteger('42') AS r          // 42
RETURN toIntegerList(['1', '2', 'x']) AS r  // [1, 2, null]

docs.title: Null Propagation
docs.text:
Every numeric function returns null when any argument is null, so they compose safely over optional data:

MATCH (n:Product)
RETURN n.name AS name, round(sqrt(n.score)) AS rating

docs.title: Cypher Query Language
docs.text: GrafitoDB includes a complete Cypher parser and executor, allowing you to use Neo4j-style declarative queries.

docs.title: What is Cypher?
docs.text:
Cypher is a declarative graph query language that describes patterns in graphs using ASCII-art notation.

// Find Alice's friends
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Alice'})-[:KNOWS]->(friend)
RETURN friend.name

docs.title: Why Use Cypher?
docs.text: Approach Best For Programmatic API Simple CRUD, dynamic queries Cypher Complex patterns, analytics, reporting

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
// Any node
(n)

// Node with label
(p:Person)

// Node with multiple labels
(p:Person:Employee)

// Node with variable and label
(a:Person)

// Anonymous node
(:Person)

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
// Directed relationship
(a)-[:KNOWS]->(b)

// Relationship with properties
(a)-[:KNOWS {since: 2020}]->(b)

// Anonymous relationship
(a)-->(b)

// Bidirectional (matches both directions)
(a)-[:KNOWS]-(b)

docs.title: Paths
docs.text:
// Two-hop path
(a)-[:KNOWS]->()-[:WORKS_AT]->(c)

// Variable-length path
(a)-[:KNOWS*1..3]->(b)

// Named path
path = (a)-[:KNOWS*]->(b)

docs.title: Executing Cypher in Grafito
docs.text:
from grafito import GrafitoDatabase

db = GrafitoDatabase(':memory:')

# Execute without results
db.execute("CREATE (n:Person {name: 'Alice'})")

# Execute with results
results = db.execute("MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n.name")
for row in results:
    print(row['n.name'])

docs.title: Query Parameters
docs.text:
Pass runtime values with $name parameters instead of interpolating them into the query string. Parameters bind in WHERE, pattern properties, RETURN and CREATE:

# Second argument is a dict of parameter values.
db.execute(
    "MATCH (n:Person {name: $name}) RETURN n.age AS age",
    {"name": "Alice"},
)

db.execute(
    "CREATE (n:Person {name: $name, age: $age})",
    {"name": "Zoe", "age": 40},
)

This avoids manual quote-escaping and the injection risk of building queries with f-strings. A referenced parameter that is not provided raises an error.

docs.title: Query Structure
docs.text:
A typical Cypher query has this structure:

[USE]           // Graph selection (not in Grafito)
[READING]       // MATCH, OPTIONAL MATCH
[PROJECTING]    // WITH
[READING]       // Additional MATCH
[WHERE]         // Filters
[PROJECTING]    // RETURN
[ORDER BY]      // Sorting
[SKIP]          // Pagination
[LIMIT]         // Pagination

docs.title: Clauses Overview
docs.text: Clause Purpose Example MATCH Find patterns MATCH (n:Person) CREATE Create nodes/relationships CREATE (n:Person) MERGE Find or create MERGE (n:Person {email: 'a@b'}) SET Update properties SET n.name = 'Alice' DELETE Remove nodes/relationships DELETE n REMOVE Remove labels/properties REMOVE n:OldLabel RETURN Define output RETURN n.name WHERE Filter results WHERE n.age > 25 ORDER BY Sort results ORDER BY n.name ASC SKIP Skip N results SKIP 10 LIMIT Limit results LIMIT 10 UNION Combine results ... UNION ... CALL Execute procedures CALL db.vector.search(...)

docs.title: Create Data
docs.text:
db.execute("""
    CREATE (a:Person {name: 'Alice', age: 30}),
           (b:Person {name: 'Bob', age: 25}),
           (a)-[:KNOWS {since: 2020}]->(b)
""")

docs.title: Query Patterns
docs.text:
# Find all persons
results = db.execute("MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n.name")

# Find specific person
results = db.execute("MATCH (n:Person {name: 'Alice'}) RETURN n")

# Find relationships
results = db.execute("""
    MATCH (a:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->(b:Person)
    RETURN a.name, b.name, r.since
""")

docs.title: Update Data
docs.text:
# Update property
db.execute("""
    MATCH (n:Person {name: 'Alice'})
    SET n.age = 31
""")

# Add label
db.execute("""
    MATCH (n:Person {name: 'Alice'})
    SET n:Employee
""")

# Remove property
db.execute("""
    MATCH (n:Person)
    REMOVE n.temporary
""")

docs.title: Delete Data
docs.text:
# Delete relationship
db.execute("""
    MATCH (a)-[r:KNOWS]->(b)
    WHERE a.name = 'Alice'
    DELETE r
""")

# Delete node (and its relationships)
db.execute("""
    MATCH (n:Person {name: 'Alice'})
    DELETE n
""")

# Delete everything (careful!)
db.execute("MATCH (n) DETACH DELETE n")

docs.title: Variable-Length Paths
docs.text:
Configure default max hops when creating the database:

db = GrafitoDatabase(':memory:', cypher_max_hops=5)

# Unbounded uses default max
db.execute("MATCH (a)-[:KNOWS*..]->(b) RETURN b")

# Explicit bounds
db.execute("MATCH (a)-[:KNOWS*1..3]->(b) RETURN b")

docs.title: Result Format
docs.text:
Query results are returned as a list of dictionaries:

results = db.execute("""
    MATCH (n:Person)
    RETURN n.name, n.age
""")

for row in results:
    print(f"Name: {row['n.name']}")
    print(f"Age: {row['n.age']}")

With aliases:

results = db.execute("""
    MATCH (n:Person)
    RETURN n.name AS name, n.age AS age
""")

for row in results:
    print(f"{row['name']}: {row['age']}")

docs.title: Hybrid Usage
docs.text:
Mix Cypher with the programmatic API:

# Create with API
alice = db.create_node(labels=['Person'], properties={'name': 'Alice'})

# Query with Cypher
results = db.execute("MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n")

# Update with Cypher (use a parameter instead of interpolating the value)
db.execute("MATCH (n) WHERE id(n) = $id SET n.active = true", {"id": alice.id})

# Verify with API
updated = db.get_node(alice.id)
print(updated.properties['active'])  # True

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• CREATE and MATCH
  • Filtering with WHERE
  • Return and Aggregation
  • Data Modification
  • Complex Patterns

docs.title: Complex Patterns
docs.text: Advanced pattern matching techniques.

docs.title: Matching Separate Patterns
docs.text:
// Match multiple independent patterns
MATCH
  (a:Person {name: 'Alice'}),
  (b:Person {name: 'Bob'})
RETURN a, b

docs.title: Connecting Patterns
docs.text:
// Alice knows someone who knows Bob
MATCH
  (a:Person {name: 'Alice'})-[:KNOWS]->(friend),
  (friend)-[:KNOWS]->(b:Person {name: 'Bob'})
RETURN friend.name

docs.title: Multiple Path Patterns
docs.text:
// Find common connections through different paths
MATCH
  (a:Person)-[:WORKS_AT]->(c:Company),
  (a)-[:LIVES_IN]->(city:City)
RETURN a.name, c.name, city.name

docs.title: OPTIONAL MATCH
docs.text: Returns NULL for missing parts instead of filtering out.

docs.title: Basic Optional Match
docs.text:
// Get all persons, with their company if they have one
MATCH (p:Person)
OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:WORKS_AT]->(c:Company)
RETURN p.name, c.name  // c.name is NULL if no company

docs.title: Multiple Optionals
docs.text:
// Person with optional company and optional location
MATCH (p:Person)
OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:WORKS_AT]->(c:Company)
OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:LIVES_IN]->(city:City)
RETURN p.name, c.name, city.name

docs.title: Optional with WHERE
docs.text:
MATCH (p:Person)
OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:KNOWS]->(friend)
WHERE friend.active = true
RETURN p.name, friend.name

docs.title: Self-Referencing
docs.text:
// Find mutual relationships
MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(a)
RETURN a.name, b.name

docs.title: Triangles
docs.text:
// Find friend triangles (A knows B, B knows C, C knows A)
MATCH
  (a)-[:KNOWS]->(b),
  (b)-[:KNOWS]->(c),
  (c)-[:KNOWS]->(a)
RETURN a.name, b.name, c.name

docs.title: Capturing Paths
docs.text:
// Capture entire path
MATCH p = (a:Person)-[:KNOWS*1..3]->(b:Person)
WHERE a.name = 'Alice' AND b.name = 'Bob'
RETURN p, length(p) as hops

docs.title: Path Functions
docs.text:
// Analyze paths
MATCH p = (a)-[:KNOWS*]->(b)
RETURN
  nodes(p) as pathNodes,
  relationships(p) as pathRels,
  length(p) as numHops

docs.title: Basic Comprehension
docs.text:
// Collect friends into a list
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Alice'})
RETURN [(a)-[:KNOWS]->(b) | b.name] as friends

docs.title: With Filter
docs.text:
// Only active friends
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Alice'})
RETURN [(a)-[:KNOWS]->(b) WHERE b.active | b.name] as activeFriends

docs.title: Multi-Element Patterns
docs.text:
// Get friends and their companies
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Alice'})
RETURN [(a)-[:KNOWS]->(b)-[:WORKS_AT]->(c) | {friend: b.name, company: c.name}] as connections

docs.title: RETURN and Aggregation
docs.text: Transform and aggregate query results.

docs.title: Returning Nodes
docs.text:
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN p

docs.title: Returning Properties
docs.text:
// Single property
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN p.name

// Multiple properties
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN p.name, p.age, p.email

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
// Using AS keyword
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN p.name AS personName, p.age AS years

// Implicit alias (without AS - not recommended)
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN p.name personName

docs.title: Distinct Results
docs.text:
// Remove duplicates
MATCH (p:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(friend)
RETURN DISTINCT friend.name

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text:
// Computed values
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN p.name, p.age + 1 AS nextYearAge

// String concatenation
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN p.firstName + ' ' + p.lastName AS fullName

Arithmetic uses + - * / % ^ with standard precedence; see Numeric Functions.

docs.title: Standalone RETURN
docs.text:
A query can consist of just a RETURN (no MATCH), which is handy for evaluating expressions:

RETURN 1 + 1 AS x            // [{'x': 2}]
RETURN toUpper('abc') AS x   // [{'x': 'ABC'}]

docs.title: COUNT
docs.text:
// Count all matches
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN COUNT(p) AS personCount

// Count non-NULL values
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN COUNT(p.email) AS withEmail

// Count all rows (including NULLs)
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN COUNT(*) AS total

// Count distinct
MATCH (p:Person)-[:WORKS_AT]->(c:Company)
RETURN COUNT(DISTINCT c.name) AS companyCount

docs.title: SUM
docs.text:
// Total of all ages
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN SUM(p.age) AS totalAge

// Total salary by department
MATCH (e:Employee)
RETURN e.department, SUM(e.salary) AS totalSalary

docs.title: AVG
docs.text:
// Average age
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN AVG(p.age) AS averageAge

// Average by group
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN p.city, AVG(p.age) AS avgAge

docs.title: MIN / MAX
docs.text:
// Minimum and maximum
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN MIN(p.age) AS youngest, MAX(p.age) AS oldest

// By city
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN p.city, MIN(p.age), MAX(p.age)

docs.title: COLLECT
docs.text:
// Collect into list
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN COLLECT(p.name) AS allNames

// Collect with filter
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.city = 'NYC'
RETURN COLLECT(p.name) AS nyNames

// Nested collect
MATCH (p:Person)-[:WORKS_AT]->(c:Company)
RETURN c.name, COLLECT(p.name) AS employees

docs.title: Standard Deviation
docs.text:
// Sample standard deviation
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN stdDev(p.age) AS ageStdDev

// Population standard deviation
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN stdDevP(p.age) AS agePopulationStdDev

docs.title: Percentiles
docs.text:
// Continuous percentile (interpolated)
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN percentileCont(p.age, 0.5) AS medianAge

// Discrete percentile (actual value)
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN percentileDisc(p.age, 0.9) AS p90Age

docs.title: Implicit Grouping
docs.text:
// Group by company
MATCH (p:Person)-[:WORKS_AT]->(c:Company)
RETURN c.name, AVG(p.age) AS avgAge

// Multiple group keys
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN p.city, p.department, COUNT(*) AS count

docs.title: WITH for Pre-aggregation
docs.text:
// Filter after aggregation
MATCH (p:Person)
WITH p.city AS city, COUNT(*) AS cityCount
WHERE cityCount > 10
RETURN city, cityCount

docs.title: Conditional Values
docs.text:
// Using CASE
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN p.name,
CASE
  WHEN p.age < 18 THEN 'minor'
  WHEN p.age < 65 THEN 'adult'
  ELSE 'senior'
END AS category

docs.title: Complex Expressions
docs.text:
// Computed columns
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN
  p.name,
  p.age,
  p.age * 12 AS ageInMonths,
  date().year - p.birthYear AS calculatedAge

docs.title: Returning Maps
docs.text:
// Create map from properties
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN {
  name: p.name,
  age: p.age,
  city: p.city
} AS personMap

docs.title: Returning Paths
docs.text:
// Return full path
MATCH p = (a:Person)-[:KNOWS*1..3]->(b:Person)
RETURN p, length(p) AS hops

// Path nodes and relationships
MATCH p = (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b:Person)
RETURN nodes(p) AS pathNodes, relationships(p) AS pathRels

docs.title: nodes()
docs.text:
Returns a list of all nodes in a path.

MATCH p = (a:Person {name: 'Alice'})-[:KNOWS*1..3]->(b:Person)
RETURN nodes(p) as pathNodes
// [(:Person {name: 'Alice'}), (:Person {...}), ...]

// Count nodes in path
MATCH p = shortestPath((a)-[:KNOWS*]-(b))
RETURN size(nodes(p)) as nodeCount

docs.title: relationships()
docs.text:
Returns a list of all relationships in a path.

MATCH p = (a:Person {name: 'Alice'})-[:KNOWS*1..3]->(b:Person)
RETURN relationships(p) as pathRels
// [(:KNOWS {...}), (:KNOWS {...}), ...]

// Get relationship types
MATCH p = (a)-[*1..3]-(b)
RETURN [r IN relationships(p) | type(r)] as relTypes

docs.title: length()
docs.text:
Returns the number of relationships in a path. length() also accepts a string or list and returns its length.

MATCH p = (a)-[:KNOWS*]->(b)
RETURN length(p) as hops

docs.title: Graph and Scalar Functions
docs.text:
These functions inspect nodes and relationships:

Function Returns labels(n) List of a node's labels type(r) A relationship's type properties(x) Property map of a node/relationship (or the map itself) keys(x) List of property names id(x) Integer identity of a node/relationship elementId(x) Identity as a string startNode(r) / endNode(r) The source / target node of a relationship 
MATCH (n:Person {name: 'Alice'})
RETURN labels(n) AS labels, properties(n) AS props, id(n) AS id

MATCH ()-[r]->()
RETURN type(r) AS rel_type, startNode(r).name AS from, endNode(r).name AS to

labels() can also be used as a filter, e.g. WHERE 'Admin' IN labels(n).

docs.title: Dashboard Metrics
docs.text:
// User statistics
MATCH (u:User)
RETURN
  COUNT(*) AS totalUsers,
  COUNT(u.verifiedEmail) AS verifiedUsers,
  AVG(u.loginCount) AS avgLogins,
  MAX(u.lastLogin) AS mostRecentLogin

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
// Monthly signups
MATCH (u:User)
WITH date.truncate('month', u.createdAt) AS month, COUNT(*) AS signups
RETURN month, signups
ORDER BY month

docs.title: Network Analysis
docs.text:
// Most connected people
MATCH (p:Person)
WITH p, COUNT { (p)-[:KNOWS]-() } AS connections
RETURN p.name, connections
ORDER BY connections DESC
LIMIT 10

docs.title: String Functions
docs.text: String manipulation functions in Cypher.

docs.title: toInteger()
docs.text:
Converts a value to an integer.

// From string
RETURN toInteger('42')        // 42
RETURN toInteger('3.14')      // 3 (truncates)

// From float
RETURN toInteger(3.9)         // 3 (truncates)

// From boolean
RETURN toInteger(true)        // 1
RETURN toInteger(false)       // 0

// Null handling
RETURN toInteger(null)        // null

docs.title: toFloat()
docs.text:
Converts a value to a float.

// From string
RETURN toFloat('3.14')        // 3.14
RETURN toFloat('2')           // 2.0

// From integer
RETURN toFloat(42)            // 42.0

// From boolean
RETURN toFloat(true)          // 1.0
RETURN toFloat(false)         // 0.0

// Null handling
RETURN toFloat(null)          // null

docs.title: toString()
docs.text:
Converts any value to a string.

// From number
RETURN toString(42)           // '42'
RETURN toString(3.14)         // '3.14'

// From boolean
RETURN toString(true)         // 'true'
RETURN toString(false)        // 'false'

// From temporal types
RETURN toString(date())       // '2024-01-15'
RETURN toString(datetime())   // '2024-01-15T14:30:00.123456'

// Null handling
RETURN toString(null)         // 'null'

docs.title: toBoolean()
docs.text:
Converts a string or integer to a boolean. 'true'/'false' are matched case-insensitively; an integer is false when 0 and true otherwise. A string that is neither 'true' nor 'false' returns null.

RETURN toBoolean('TRUE')   // true
RETURN toBoolean('false')  // false
RETURN toBoolean('maybe')  // null
RETURN toBoolean(1)        // true

docs.title: List Casting
docs.text:
toIntegerList(), toFloatList(), toStringList(), and toBooleanList() cast each element of a list. An element that cannot be converted becomes null (rather than raising an error).

RETURN toIntegerList(['1', '2', 'x'])      // [1, 2, null]
RETURN toFloatList(['1.5', '2'])           // [1.5, 2.0]
RETURN toStringList([1, 2])                // ['1', '2']
RETURN toBooleanList(['true', 'nope', 'false'])  // [true, null, false]

docs.title: toUpper()
docs.text:
// Convert to uppercase
RETURN toUpper('hello')  // 'HELLO'

// With null
RETURN toUpper(null)  // null

docs.title: toLower()
docs.text:
// Convert to lowercase
RETURN toLower('HELLO')  // 'hello'

// Mixed case
RETURN toLower('Hello World')  // 'hello world'

docs.title: trim()
docs.text:
// Remove leading and trailing whitespace
RETURN trim('  hello  ')  // 'hello'
RETURN trim('\thello\n')  // 'hello'

docs.title: ltrim() / rtrim()
docs.text:
Trim whitespace from only the left or right side.

RETURN ltrim('  hi')  // 'hi'
RETURN rtrim('hi  ')  // 'hi'

docs.title: replace()
docs.text:
Replace every occurrence of a substring.

RETURN replace('abcabc', 'a', 'X')  // 'XbcXbc'

docs.title: left() / right()
docs.text:
Take the first or last n characters.

RETURN left('hello', 2)   // 'he'
RETURN right('hello', 2)  // 'lo'

docs.title: reverse()
docs.text:
reverse() preserves the input type: a string reverses to a string, a list to a list.

RETURN reverse('abc')        // 'cba'
RETURN reverse([1, 2, 3])    // [3, 2, 1]

docs.title: substring()
docs.text:
// substring(text, start, length?)

// From position 0, length 3
RETURN substring('Hello', 0, 3)  // 'Hel'

// From position 1, length 3
RETURN substring('Hello', 1, 3)  // 'ell'

// From position to end (no length)
RETURN substring('Hello', 2)  // 'llo'

// Negative start is not allowed
// substring('Hello', -1)  // ERROR

docs.title: split()
docs.text:
// Split by delimiter
RETURN split('a,b,c', ',')  // ['a', 'b', 'c']

// Split by space
RETURN split('hello world', ' ')  // ['hello', 'world']

// Split with empty strings
RETURN split('a,,c', ',')  // ['a', '', 'c']

// Wrong type raises error
// RETURN split(123, ',')  // CypherExecutionError

docs.title: regex()
docs.text:
Returns boolean if pattern matches anywhere in string.

// Simple match
RETURN regex('abc', 'a.c')  // true

// Any character
RETURN regex('hello', 'h.*o')  // true

// Character class
RETURN regex('abc', '[aeiou]')  // true

// No match
RETURN regex('abc', '^d')  // false

// Invalid pattern raises error
// RETURN regex('abc', '[')  // CypherExecutionError

docs.title: matches()
docs.text:
Returns boolean for full string match (implied ^ and $).

// Full match
RETURN matches('abc', 'abc')  // true

// Pattern must match entire string
RETURN matches('abc', 'a')  // false
RETURN matches('abc', 'a.*')  // true

// Digit pattern
RETURN matches('123', '\\d+')  // true

docs.title: Using + Operator
docs.text:
// Concatenate with +
WITH 'Hello' as a, 'World' as b
RETURN a + ' ' + b  // 'Hello World'

// With numbers (converted to string)
RETURN 'Count: ' + 42  // 'Count: 42'

docs.title: apoc.text.join()
docs.text:
// Join list with separator
RETURN apoc.text.join(['a', 'b', 'c'], ',')  // 'a,b,c'
RETURN apoc.text.join(['2024', '01', '15'], '-')  // '2024-01-15'

docs.title: deaccent()
docs.text:
Remove accents from characters.

// Remove accents
RETURN deaccent('café')  // 'cafe'
RETURN deaccent('naïve')  // 'naive'
RETURN deaccent('résumé')  // 'resume'

// No accents = no change
RETURN deaccent('hello')  // 'hello'

// Null handling
RETURN deaccent(null)  // null

docs.title: strip_html()
docs.text:
Remove HTML tags from text.

// Strip HTML tags
RETURN strip_html('<p>Hello <b>World</b></p>')  // 'Hello World'
RETURN strip_html('<div>Text</div>')  // 'Text'

// Already plain text = no change
RETURN strip_html('plain text')  // 'plain text'

// Null handling
RETURN strip_html(null)  // null

docs.title: strip_emoji()
docs.text:
Remove emoji characters from text.

// Remove emojis
RETURN strip_emoji('Hello 😀 World 🌍')  // 'Hello  World '
RETURN strip_emoji('Great job 👍👍')  // 'Great job '

// No emojis = no change
RETURN strip_emoji('Hello World')  // 'Hello World'

// Null handling
RETURN strip_emoji(null)  // null

docs.title: snake_case()
docs.text:
Convert text to snake_case format.

// Convert to snake_case
RETURN snake_case('Hello World')  // 'hello_world'
RETURN snake_case('helloWorld')  // 'hello_world'
RETURN snake_case('HelloWorld')  // 'hello_world'
RETURN snake_case('hello-world')  // 'hello_world'
RETURN snake_case('hello_world')  // 'hello_world'

// Multiple words
RETURN snake_case('The Quick Brown Fox')  // 'the_quick_brown_fox'

// Null handling
RETURN snake_case(null)  // null

docs.title: levenshtein()
docs.text:
Calculate Levenshtein (edit) distance between two strings.

// Exact match
RETURN levenshtein('hello', 'hello')  // 0

// One character different
RETURN levenshtein('hello', 'hallo')  // 1

// Two edits needed
RETURN levenshtein('kitten', 'sitting')  // 3

// Case sensitive
RETURN levenshtein('Hello', 'hello')  // 1

// Use with deaccent for fuzzy matching
RETURN levenshtein(deaccent('café'), 'cafe')  // 0

// Null handling
RETURN levenshtein(null, 'hello')  // null
RETURN levenshtein('hello', null)  // null

Common use case - fuzzy search:

// Find similar names
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE levenshtein(deaccent(p.name), 'john') <= 2
RETURN p.name

docs.title: jaccard()
docs.text:
Calculate Jaccard similarity coefficient between two strings (based on character bigrams).

// Similar strings
RETURN jaccard('hello', 'hello')  // 1.0
RETURN jaccard('hello', 'hallo')  // ~0.6

// Different strings
RETURN jaccard('hello', 'world')  // 0.0

// Partial similarity
RETURN jaccard('night', 'nacht')  // ~0.3

// Null handling
RETURN jaccard(null, 'hello')  // null

Use for similarity matching:

// Find potential duplicates
MATCH (p1:Person), (p2:Person)
WHERE p1.id < p2.id
  AND jaccard(p1.name, p2.name) > 0.8
RETURN p1.name, p2.name, jaccard(p1.name, p2.name) as similarity

docs.title: size() with Strings
docs.text:
// String length
RETURN size('Hello')  // 5
RETURN size('')  // 0

docs.title: starts WITH / ends WITH / contains
docs.text:
In WHERE clause:

// Starts with
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.name STARTS WITH 'Al'
RETURN p.name

// Ends with
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.email ENDS WITH '@company.com'
RETURN p.name

// Contains
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.bio CONTAINS 'engineer'
RETURN p.name

docs.title: Replace
docs.text:
apoc.text.replace() treats its pattern as a regular expression (unlike the native replace() which matches a literal substring).

RETURN apoc.text.replace('hello-world', '-', '_')  // 'hello_world'

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
All string functions return null for null input:

RETURN toUpper(null)      // null
RETURN trim(null)         // null
RETURN substring(null, 0) // null
RETURN split(null, ',')   // null
RETURN deaccent(null)     // null
RETURN strip_html(null)   // null
RETURN strip_emoji(null)  // null
RETURN snake_case(null)   // null
RETURN levenshtein(null, 'a')  // null
RETURN jaccard(null, 'a')    // null

Invalid argument types raise CypherExecutionError:

// These raise errors:
RETURN substring('abc', 0, -1)  // Negative length
RETURN split(123, ',')          // Number instead of string
RETURN regex('abc', '[')        // Invalid regex pattern

docs.title: Normalizing Input
docs.text:
// Clean user input for search
WITH '  John DOE  ' as raw
RETURN snake_case(deaccent(trim(raw))) as clean
// 'john_doe'

docs.title: Email Domain Extraction
docs.text:
WITH 'alice@company.com' as email
RETURN split(email, '@')[1] as domain
// 'company.com'

docs.title: Name Formatting
docs.text:
// Format: Last, First
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN substring(p.lastName, 0, 1) + '. ' + p.firstName as display

docs.title: Fuzzy Matching
docs.text:
// Find similar names with multiple strategies
MATCH (p:Person)
WITH p, deaccent(p.name) as normalized
WHERE levenshtein(normalized, 'johnson') <= 2
   OR jaccard(normalized, 'johnson') > 0.7
RETURN p.name

docs.title: Content Cleaning
docs.text:
// Clean article content for indexing
MATCH (a:Article)
SET a.clean_content = strip_emoji(strip_html(a.raw_content))

docs.title: Duplicate Detection
docs.text:
// Find potential duplicate companies
MATCH (c1:Company), (c2:Company)
WHERE c1.id < c2.id
  AND jaccard(
    snake_case(deaccent(c1.name)),
    snake_case(deaccent(c2.name))
  ) > 0.85
RETURN c1.name, c2.name

docs.title: Temporal and Spatial Types
docs.text: Working with time and space in Cypher.

docs.title: Date
docs.text:
// Create date
RETURN date('2024-01-15') as d

// From components
RETURN date({year: 2024, month: 1, day: 15}) as d

// Current date
RETURN date() as today

docs.title: Time
docs.text:
// Create time
RETURN time('14:30:00') as t
RETURN time('14:30:00.123') as t
RETURN time('14:30:00+01:00') as t  // with timezone

// Current time
RETURN time() as now

docs.title: LocalTime
docs.text:
Time without timezone information.

// Create local time
RETURN localtime('14:30:00') as t
RETURN localtime('14:30:00.123') as t

// Current local time
RETURN localtime() as now

// From string with timezone (timezone is discarded)
RETURN localtime('14:30:00+05:00')  // 14:30:00

docs.title: DateTime
docs.text:
// Full datetime
RETURN datetime('2024-01-15T14:30:00') as dt

// With timezone
RETURN datetime('2024-01-15T14:30:00Z') as dt  // UTC
RETURN datetime('2024-01-15T14:30:00+05:00') as dt

// Current datetime
RETURN datetime() as now

docs.title: LocalDateTime
docs.text:
DateTime without timezone information.

// From ISO string (without timezone)
RETURN localdatetime('2024-01-15T14:30:00') as ldt

// Current local datetime
RETURN localdatetime() as now

// From string with timezone (timezone is discarded)
RETURN localdatetime('2024-01-15T14:30:00+05:00')  // 2024-01-15T14:30:00

Timezone handling

When parsing a string with timezone using localdatetime(), the timezone offset is discarded and the local time is preserved. Use datetime() if you need to preserve timezone information.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text:
// ISO duration format
RETURN duration('P1Y2M3DT4H5M6S') as dur  // 1 year, 2 months, 3 days, 4 hours...
RETURN duration('P1D') as oneDay
RETURN duration('PT2H30M') as twoHalfHours

// From components
RETURN duration({days: 1, hours: 2}) as dur

docs.title: Comparisons
docs.text:
// Compare dates
WITH date('2024-01-15') as d1, date('2024-01-20') as d2
RETURN d1 < d2  // true

// Range queries
MATCH (p:Person)
WHERE p.birthday >= date('1990-01-01')
  AND p.birthday <= date('1999-12-31')
RETURN p.name

docs.title: Arithmetic
docs.text:
// Add duration to date
RETURN date('2024-01-15') + duration('P1M')  // 2024-02-15

// Subtract from datetime
RETURN datetime() - duration('P7D')  // 1 week ago

// Duration between dates
RETURN duration.between(
  date('2024-01-01'),
  date('2024-01-15')
)  // P14D

docs.title: Truncation
docs.text:
// Truncate to year/month/day
RETURN date.truncate('year', date('2024-06-15'))   // 2024-01-01
RETURN date.truncate('month', date('2024-06-15'))  // 2024-06-01

// Truncate datetime
RETURN datetime.truncate('hour', datetime())  // Current hour, minute=0, second=0

docs.title: Accessing Components
docs.text:
WITH date('2024-01-15') as d
RETURN d.year   // 2024
RETURN d.month  // 1
RETURN d.day    // 15
RETURN d.week   // 3 (week of year)
RETURN d.dayOfWeek  // 1 (Monday)
RETURN d.quarter    // 1

docs.title: Converting Between Types
docs.text:
// Date to datetime
RETURN datetime(date('2024-01-15'))  // 2024-01-15T00:00:00

// Datetime to date
RETURN date(datetime('2024-01-15T14:30:00'))  // 2024-01-15

// String to temporal
RETURN date('2024-01-15')
RETURN time('14:30:00')

docs.title: Point (2D)
docs.text:
// Create point with x, y
RETURN point({x: 10, y: 20}) as p

// Create geographic point
RETURN point({longitude: -74.006, latitude: 40.7128}) as nyc

docs.title: Distance
docs.text:
// Euclidean distance
WITH point({x: 0, y: 0}) as p1, point({x: 3, y: 4}) as p2
RETURN distance(p1, p2)  // 5.0

// Geographic distance (in meters)
WITH
  point({longitude: -74.006, latitude: 40.7128}) as nyc,
  point({longitude: -118.2437, latitude: 34.0522}) as la
RETURN distance(nyc, la) as meters

docs.title: Accessing Components
docs.text:
WITH point({x: 10, y: 20}) as p
RETURN p.x, p.y

WITH point({longitude: -74.006, latitude: 40.7128}) as p
RETURN p.longitude, p.latitude

docs.title: Age Calculation
docs.text:
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN p.name,
       duration.between(p.birthday, date()).years as age

docs.title: Recent Activity
docs.text:
// Users active in last 7 days
MATCH (u:User)
WHERE u.lastLogin > datetime() - duration('P7D')
RETURN u.name

docs.title: Geographic Search
docs.text:
// Find locations within radius
MATCH (store:Store)
WITH store, point({longitude: store.lon, latitude: store.lat}) as storePoint
WITH store, storePoint,
     point({longitude: -74.006, latitude: 40.7128}) as center
WHERE distance(storePoint, center) < 5000  // within 5km
RETURN store.name

docs.title: Time-Based Aggregation
docs.text:
// Group by month
MATCH (o:Order)
WITH date.truncate('month', o.createdAt) as month, count(*) as orders
RETURN month, orders
ORDER BY month

docs.title: Vector Search in Cypher
docs.text: Perform semantic search using Cypher procedures.

docs.title: Vector Search Procedure
docs.text:
CALL db.vector.search(
    index_name,      // Name of vector index
    query_vector,    // Vector to search for
    k,               // Number of results
    options          // Optional configuration
)
YIELD node, score

docs.title: Basic Vector Search
docs.text:
from grafito.cypher import format_vector_literal

# Prepare query vector
query_vec = model.encode("python graph database").tolist()
vector_literal = format_vector_literal(query_vec, precision=8)

# Run vector search
cypher = f"""
    CALL db.vector.search('articles_vec', {vector_literal}, 10)
    YIELD node, score
    RETURN node.title, node.content, score
    ORDER BY score DESC
"""

results = db.execute(cypher)

docs.title: With Label Filters
docs.text:
// Search only within specific labels
CALL db.vector.search(
    'articles_vec',
    [0.123, -0.456, ...],
    10,
    {labels: ['Article', 'Tutorial']}
)
YIELD node, score
RETURN node.title, score

docs.title: With Property Filters
docs.text:
// Search with property constraints
CALL db.vector.search(
    'articles_vec',
    [0.123, -0.456, ...],
    10,
    {
        labels: ['Article'],
        properties: {published: true, language: 'en'}
    }
)
YIELD node, score
RETURN node.title, score

docs.title: With Reranking
docs.text:
// Enable reranking with stored vectors
CALL db.vector.search(
    'articles_vec',
    [0.123, -0.456, ...],
    10,
    {rerank: true, candidate_multiplier: 3}
)
YIELD node, score
RETURN node.title, score

docs.title: Custom Reranker
docs.text:
# Register custom reranker
def my_reranker(query_vector, candidates):
    # candidates: [{"id": int, "vector": [...], "score": float, "node": Node}, ...]
    re_ranked = []
    for c in candidates:
        # Custom scoring logic
        boost = 1.0
        if 'featured' in c['node'].labels:
            boost = 1.2
        re_ranked.append({
            'id': c['id'],
            'score': c['score'] * boost
        })
    return re_ranked

db.register_reranker('featured_boost', my_reranker)

// Use in Cypher
CALL db.vector.search(
    'articles_vec',
    [0.123, -0.456, ...],
    10,
    {reranker: 'featured_boost'}
)
YIELD node, score
RETURN node.title, score

docs.title: Aliasing YIELD Outputs
docs.text:
YIELD accepts AS to rename an output. The alias is a real pattern variable, so it can be matched on directly:

CALL db.vector.search('articles_vec', $query_vec, 10) YIELD node AS article, score AS relevance
MATCH (article)<-[:AUTHORED]-(author:Person)
RETURN article.title, author.name, relevance
ORDER BY relevance DESC

Without AS, the outputs keep their procedure names (node, score) — which collide if you call the procedure twice in one query. Aliasing is what makes the two-endpoint pattern below possible.

docs.title: Semantic Predicates
docs.text:
db.vector.search answers "which nodes are closest?". Sometimes you already have a node from a pattern match and need the opposite question: "how close is this node?". Two functions score a node against a query:

VECTOR_SCORE(node, query)                 // the raw similarity score, or NULL
SIMILAR(node, query)                      // score >= default threshold (0.5)
SIMILAR(node, query, 0.75)                // score >= 0.75
SIMILAR(node, query, {index: 'articles_vec', min_score: 0.75})

query is either a vector literal/parameter or a string, which is embedded with the index's embedding function. Each distinct query string is embedded once per execution, not once per candidate row.

Options:

Option Meaning Default index Vector index to score against 'default' min_score Threshold for SIMILAR 0.5

Semantics worth knowing:

  • A node with no embedding in the index scores NULL under VECTOR_SCORE and false under SIMILAR — an unindexed node is dropped by the filter rather than propagating unknown through it.
  • A NULL node (from OPTIONAL MATCH) yields NULL for both.
  • Scores follow the index metric and are always "higher is better": cosine in [-1, 1], inner product unbounded, and negated squared distance (<= 0) for l2. Because the default threshold is calibrated for cosine, SIMILAR on an l2 index requires an explicit min_score rather than silently matching nothing.

These are predicates, not seeks

SIMILAR and VECTOR_SCORE score the node they are handed; they never consult the ANN index for neighbours. Filtering a bare MATCH (n) with them scans and scores every node in the database:

// Slow: full scan, one score per node
MATCH (n) WHERE SIMILAR(n, 'transformers') RETURN n

Seed the pattern with db.vector.search — which does use the index — and use SIMILAR only to constrain an already-bounded set:

// Fast: ANN picks 20 candidates, SIMILAR filters the far end
CALL db.vector.search('articles_vec', 'transformers', 20) YIELD node AS a
MATCH (a)-[:CITES]->(b)
WHERE SIMILAR(b, 'attention mechanism', 0.7)
RETURN a.title, b.title

docs.title: Deep Graph Search
docs.text:
Because YIELD aliases bind as pattern variables, both ends of a path can be seeded semantically — finding paths whose endpoints are similar to two concepts, rather than searching for one concept and then the other:

CALL db.vector.search('articles_vec', 'chatgpt', 10) YIELD node AS a
CALL db.vector.search('articles_vec', 'anthropic', 10) YIELD node AS b
MATCH p=(a)-[*1..3]->(b)
RETURN p
LIMIT 10

The second CALL runs per row from the first, so the pattern explores every pairing of the two candidate sets. Keep both k values modest — the path search is quadratic in them.

To score how strongly each endpoint matched, keep the scores:

CALL db.vector.search('papers_vec', $topic_a, 10) YIELD node AS a, score AS score_a
CALL db.vector.search('papers_vec', $topic_b, 10) YIELD node AS b, score AS score_b
MATCH p=(a)-[:CITES*1..3]->(b)
RETURN a.title, b.title, length(p) AS hops, score_a + score_b AS strength
ORDER BY strength DESC, hops ASC
LIMIT 20

docs.title: Combining with Graph Patterns
docs.text:
# Hybrid: vector search + graph traversal
query_vec = model.encode("machine learning tutorials").tolist()
vector_literal = format_vector_literal(query_vec)

cypher = f"""
    // Stage 1: Vector search for candidates
    CALL db.vector.search('articles_vec', {vector_literal}, 20)
    YIELD node, score

    // Stage 2: Expand to authors
    MATCH (node)<-[:AUTHORED]-(author:Person)

    // Stage 3: Get author's other content
    OPTIONAL MATCH (author)-[:AUTHORED]->(other:Article)
    WHERE other <> node

    RETURN 
        node.title as matched_article,
        score,
        author.name as author,
        collect(DISTINCT other.title)[0..3] as other_works
    ORDER BY score DESC
    LIMIT 10
"""

results = db.execute(cypher)

docs.title: With Path Expansion
docs.text:
// Vector search + related content
CALL db.vector.search('articles_vec', $query_vec, 5)
YIELD node, score

// Find related articles through shared tags
MATCH (node)-[:TAGGED]->(tag)<-[:TAGGED]-(related)
WHERE related <> node

RETURN 
    node.title as main_result,
    score,
    collect(DISTINCT related.title)[0..5] as related_articles
ORDER BY score DESC

docs.title: Aggregating Vector Results
docs.text:
// Cluster search results by category
CALL db.vector.search('articles_vec', $query_vec, 50)
YIELD node, score

WITH node.category as category, 
     collect({node: node, score: score}) as items,
     avg(score) as avg_score

RETURN 
    category,
    count(*) as count,
    avg_score,
    items[0..3] as top_items
ORDER BY avg_score DESC

docs.title: Dynamic Vector Queries
docs.text:
# Build vector queries dynamically
def vector_search_with_context(db, query, user_id, k=10):
    # Get user's interests
    interests = db.execute("""
        MATCH (u:User {id: $user_id})-[:INTERESTED_IN]->(topic)
        RETURN collect(topic.name) as interests
    """, {'user_id': user_id})

    # Build enriched query
    enriched_query = query + ' ' + ' '.join(interests[0]['interests'])
    query_vec = model.encode(enriched_query).tolist()

    # Search with personalization boost
    return db.execute("""
        CALL db.vector.search('articles_vec', $vec, $k)
        YIELD node, score

        // Boost if matches user interests
        OPTIONAL MATCH (node)-[:ABOUT]->(topic)
        WHERE topic.name IN $interests

        WITH node, score, count(topic) as interest_matches
        ORDER BY score + (interest_matches * 0.1) DESC

        RETURN node.title, node.summary, score
        LIMIT $k
    """, {'vec': query_vec, 'k': k, 'interests': interests[0]['interests']})

docs.title: Unknown Index
docs.text:
DatabaseError: Vector index 'unknown_idx' not found

Solution: Check index name with SHOW INDEXES or db.list_vector_indexes().

docs.title: Dimension Mismatch
docs.text:
DatabaseError: Query vector dimension 768 does not match index dimension 384

Solution: Ensure query vector has same dimension as index.

docs.title: Unknown Reranker
docs.text:
CypherExecutionError: Unknown reranker 'invalid_name'

Solution: Register reranker first with db.register_reranker().

docs.title: Use Precision Parameter
docs.text:
# Format vector for Cypher with appropriate precision
vector_literal = format_vector_literal(query_vec, precision=6)
# Higher precision = more accurate but longer query string

docs.title: Limit Initial Results
docs.text:
// Get more candidates than needed for reranking
CALL db.vector.search('idx', $vec, 50)  // Get 50
YIELD node, score
// ... filter/process ...
RETURN ...
LIMIT 10  // Return top 10

# Create property index for common filters
db.create_node_index('Article', 'published')

from grafito.embedding_functions import AmazonBedrockEmbeddingFunction

    profile_name="default",
    region_name="us-east-1",
    retries={"max_attempts": 5}
)

docs.title: Hugging Face Embeddings
docs.text:
GrafitoDB supports Hugging Face embeddings through two paths:

  • Hugging Face Inference API: hosted models via HTTP.
  • Sentence Transformers (Local): run models locally with sentence-transformers.

Both integrate with GrafitoDB's vector indexes in the same way.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: pip install httpx

docs.title: API Token
docs.text:
Grafito will read the API token from any of the following environment variables (in order):

  • HF_TOKEN
  • HUGGINGFACE_HUB_TOKEN
  • HUGGINGFACEHUB_API_TOKEN
  • HUGGINGFACE_API_KEY
export HF_TOKEN="hf_..."

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
from grafito import GrafitoDatabase
from grafito.embedding_functions import HuggingFaceEmbeddingFunction

embed_fn = HuggingFaceEmbeddingFunction(
    model_name="sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
)

db = GrafitoDatabase(":memory:")
db.create_vector_index(
    name="docs_vec",
    dim=384,
    embedding_function=embed_fn
)

node = db.create_node(labels=["Doc"], properties={"text": "Graph search"})
db.upsert_embedding(node_id=node.id, text="Graph search", index="docs_vec")

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
embed_fn = HuggingFaceEmbeddingFunction(
    model_name="sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2",
    api_key_env_var="MY_HF_TOKEN"
)

docs.title: Sentence Transformers (Local)
docs.text: Use local inference with the sentence_transformers library.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: pip install sentence_transformers

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
from grafito import GrafitoDatabase
from grafito.embedding_functions import SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction

embed_fn = SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction(
    model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2",
    device="cpu",
    normalize_embeddings=False
)

db = GrafitoDatabase(":memory:")
db.create_vector_index(
    name="docs_vec",
    dim=384,
    embedding_function=embed_fn
)

docs.title: Advanced Configuration
docs.text:
SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction accepts extra keyword arguments passed to SentenceTransformer(...) (only primitive JSON-like types are allowed):

embed_fn = SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction(
    model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2",
    device="cpu",
    normalize_embeddings=True,
    trust_remote_code=False
)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The embedding dimension is derived from the model if available.
  • normalize_embeddings=True is useful when you rely on cosine similarity.

docs.title: Ollama Embeddings (Local)
docs.text: GrafitoDB can generate embeddings locally using the Ollama embeddings API. This is ideal for offline or privacy-sensitive workloads.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Ollama installed and running on your machine
  • An embeddings-capable model pulled locally (for example: nomic-embed-text)

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: pip install httpx

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
from grafito import GrafitoDatabase
from grafito.embedding_functions import OllamaEmbeddingFunction

embed_fn = OllamaEmbeddingFunction(
    model="nomic-embed-text"
)

db = GrafitoDatabase(":memory:")
db.create_vector_index(
    name="docs_vec",
    dim=768,
    embedding_function=embed_fn
)

node = db.create_node(labels=["Doc"], properties={"text": "Local embeddings"})
db.upsert_embedding(node_id=node.id, text="Local embeddings", index="docs_vec")

docs.title: Custom Host / Remote Ollama
docs.text:
By default, Grafito uses http://localhost:11434 or the OLLAMA_HOST environment variable if set.

export OLLAMA_HOST="http://localhost:11434"

embed_fn = OllamaEmbeddingFunction(
    model="nomic-embed-text",
    base_url="http://localhost:11434"
)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The embedding dimension depends on the model you choose.
  • Ollama generates embeddings one input at a time; batch large datasets carefully.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Overview - Embedding concepts and workflows
  • Hugging Face - Local Sentence Transformers
  • Cloud Providers - Managed embedding APIs

docs.title: OpenAI Embeddings
docs.text: GrafitoDB integrates with OpenAI's embedding API to generate high-quality vector representations of text.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: OpenAI provides state-of-the-art embedding models that are: - High quality: Trained on diverse internet text - Multilingual: Support for 100+ languages - Cost-effective: Competitive pricing per token - Well-documented: Extensive community support

docs.title: Supported Models
docs.text: Model Dimensions Context Window Best For text-embedding-3-small 1536 8192 General use, cost-effective text-embedding-3-large 3072 8192 Maximum quality text-embedding-ada-002 1536 8192 Legacy model

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install grafito[openai]
# or
pip install httpx

docs.title: API Key Configuration
docs.text:
export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."

Or provide explicitly:

from grafito.embedding_functions import OpenAIEmbeddingFunction

embed_fn = OpenAIEmbeddingFunction(
    api_key="sk-..."
)

docs.title: Initialize Embedding Function
docs.text:
from grafito import GrafitoDatabase
from grafito.embedding_functions import OpenAIEmbeddingFunction

# Using default model (text-embedding-3-small)
embed_fn = OpenAIEmbeddingFunction()

# Or specify a model
embed_fn = OpenAIEmbeddingFunction(
    model="text-embedding-3-large"
)

docs.title: Create Vector Index
docs.text:
db = GrafitoDatabase(":memory:")

# Create index with OpenAI embedding function
db.create_vector_index(
    name="documents_vec",
    dim=1536,  # text-embedding-3-small
    embedding_function=embed_fn
)

docs.title: Generate Embeddings
docs.text:
# Create a document
doc = db.create_node(
    labels=["Document"],
    properties={"title": "Getting Started with Graph Databases"}
)

# Generate embedding from text
db.upsert_embedding(
    node_id=doc.id,
    text="Getting Started with Graph Databases",
    index="documents_vec"
)

docs.title: Custom Environment Variable
docs.text:
# Use a custom environment variable for the API key
embed_fn = OpenAIEmbeddingFunction(
    api_key_env_var="MY_OPENAI_KEY"
)

Then set: 

export MY_OPENAI_KEY="sk-..."

docs.title: Custom Base URL
docs.text:
For using a proxy or Azure OpenAI:

embed_fn = OpenAIEmbeddingFunction(
    model="text-embedding-3-small",
    base_url="https://your-proxy.com/v1/embeddings"
)

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
from grafito import GrafitoDatabase
from grafito.embedding_functions import OpenAIEmbeddingFunction

# Initialize embedding function
embed_fn = OpenAIEmbeddingFunction(
    model="text-embedding-3-small"
)

# Create database and index
db = GrafitoDatabase(":memory:")
db.create_vector_index(
    name="articles_vec",
    dim=1536,
    embedding_function=embed_fn,
    options={"store_embeddings": True}
)

# Add documents with embeddings
articles = [
    "Introduction to Python programming",
    "Graph databases vs relational databases",
    "Machine learning fundamentals",
    "Natural language processing techniques",
    "Data structures and algorithms"
]

for i, text in enumerate(articles):
    node = db.create_node(
        labels=["Article"],
        properties={"id": i, "content": text}
    )
    db.upsert_embedding(
        node_id=node.id,
        text=text,
        index="articles_vec"
    )

# Perform semantic search
results = db.execute("""
    CALL db.vector.search('articles_vec', 'Python coding basics', 3)
    YIELD node, score
    RETURN node.content AS content, score
""")

for result in results:
    print(f"{result['score']:.3f}: {result['content']}")

docs.title: Distance Metrics
docs.text:
OpenAI embeddings work well with multiple distance metrics:

# Cosine similarity (default)
embed_fn.default_space()  # Returns: "cosine"

# All supported spaces
embed_fn.supported_spaces()  # Returns: ["cosine", "l2", "ip"]

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
from grafito.embedding_functions import OpenAIEmbeddingFunction

try:
    embed_fn = OpenAIEmbeddingFunction()
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Missing API key: {e}")

try:
    embeddings = embed_fn(["text to embed"])
except ValueError as e:
    if "API error" in str(e):
        print(f"OpenAI API error: {e}")

docs.title: Pricing Considerations
docs.text:
OpenAI charges per token: - text-embedding-3-small: ~$0.02 per 1M tokens - text-embedding-3-large: ~$0.13 per 1M tokens

Tips to reduce costs: 1. Batch multiple texts in a single call 2. Cache embeddings for frequently used texts 3. Use text-embedding-3-small for most use cases
